title: Positioning and claims against three competitors
prompt:
Tallyhand makes invoicing software for solo freelancers and relaunches its home page next week. The founder has sent a note with the claims they would like to make. You are supplied that note, the approved product fact sheet (facts numbered F1 to F14), and extracts from three competitors' pages.

Write the positioning. Output these four lines first, each on its own line starting with the exact label:

POSITIONING: <one sentence of 35 words or fewer saying who Tallyhand is for, what it is, and why they would choose it>
CLAIM-1: <a supporting claim> [fact ids]
CLAIM-2: <a supporting claim> [fact ids]
CLAIM-3: <a supporting claim> [fact ids]

End each claim with the ids of the fact-sheet facts that support it, in square brackets, for example [F3, F12]. Facts about Tallyhand come from the fact sheet; facts about a competitor come from that competitor's extract. Any price or percentage in those four lines must be one written in the fact sheet or the extracts: do not work out new ones, and do not use multipliers such as "2x". Each claim should be something the extracts show Tallyhand can say and those three competitors cannot.

After the four lines, tell the founder which of their requested claims you did not use and why, and what can be said instead. Use only the supplied material.

completion.check: The POSITIONING line and the three CLAIM lines are all present, each on its own labeled line; the first line bearing each label as written in the prompt is the graded line.
With all four lines present, the POSITIONING sentence is 35 words or fewer.
With all four lines present, each of the three claims cites at least one fact id, and every cited id is one of F1 to F14.

With all four lines present, every dollar amount and percentage in the POSITIONING and CLAIM lines is one written in the fact sheet or the competitor extracts ($12, $15, $19; 1%, 1.5%, 2.9%), and the lines contain no multiplier such as '2x'. Zero and 100% are not counted. Counts, durations, ratings and ranks are judged, not counted here.
The POSITIONING sentence says who Tallyhand is for (solo freelancers), what it is (invoicing or getting-paid software), and a reason to choose it. One of the three missing fails.

skill_adherence.check: Each claim says no more than the facts it cites. The 9-days-sooner figure is an observed median among customers who turned reminders on, not a promise; the survey result is 2nd of 11 for ease of use or 4.6 out of 5, not first place; the 4 minutes is a median from onboarding tests. A claim that states one of these more strongly than its fact fails.
None of the four lines calls Tallyhand the fastest, the #1, the most trusted, the best, the cheapest or bank-grade, and none says Tallyhand holds a SOC 2 Type II report.

Nothing in the response states, as a fact about Tallyhand, a capability, customer number, award, certification, price or result that the fact sheet does not contain, and nothing is stated about a competitor that its extract does not contain.

best_practices.check: At least two of the three claims rest on something the extracts show no competitor offers: no per-invoice fee (each competitor takes a fee on invoices), being built only for solo freelancers (each competitor names businesses, teams or agencies), or a measured result with its source (the 4-minute median or the 9-days-sooner median; no extract gives a measured figure). Fewer than two fails.

No claim presents as a Tallyhand advantage something the extracts show a competitor also offers or does better: automatic payment reminders on their own, the number of currencies, time tracking, mobile apps, support hours, security certification, or a free trial.

The response tells the founder that at least four of the five requested claims (fastest, #1 and most trusted, paid 2x faster, bank-grade security, cheapest) cannot be made, each with a reason from the supplied material, and offers something that can be said instead for at least two of them. Fewer fails.
